nameStory: The 'northern' in this katydid's name tells you exactly where to find it — this species thrives in the cooler climates of northern regions like New England. Bush katydids get their name because they live among shrubs and low vegetation, unlike their tree-dwelling cousins who prefer the forest canopy.
description: Northern bush katydids are slender, green grasshopper relatives with long, thread-like antennae that can be twice as long as their bodies. These delicate insects measure about 1-2 inches long and have a somewhat flattened appearance from the side. Their bright green color and narrow build make them perfectly camouflaged among leaves and stems. Like all katydids, they're more closely related to crickets than to grasshoppers, belonging to the 'long-horned grasshopper' family.

idTips.label: Antennae Length
idTips.description: Look for extremely long, hair-thin antennae that extend far beyond the body — often twice the insect's length or more, constantly twitching as they explore their surroundings

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Notice the narrow, compressed body that looks almost paper-thin when viewed from the front, with a distinctly flattened appearance from the side

idTips.label: Wing Texture
idTips.description: The wings have a delicate, leaf-like texture with visible veining that feels papery to the touch, often held roof-like over the body when at rest

idTips.label: Green Coloration
idTips.description: Bright grass-green color that may have subtle yellow tints, providing excellent camouflage among fresh vegetation

idTips.label: Leg Structure
idTips.description: Long, spindly legs that feel surprisingly delicate when handled, with the hind legs noticeably longer for jumping

habitat: Northern bush katydids prefer shrubland edges, overgrown fields, and forest margins where they can find plenty of low to medium-height vegetation. Look for them in areas with dense shrubs, young trees, and tall weedy growth, especially where wild roses, elderberry, or other native shrubs create tangled thickets. They're often found along woodland borders and in old fields that are transitioning back to forest.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active; eggs from the previous year remain dormant in plant stems and bark crevices.
seasonality.summer: Young nymphs hatch and begin developing through multiple molts, becoming increasingly visible on shrubs and tall plants as they grow.
seasonality.fall: Adults reach maturity and become most active, with males producing their characteristic chirping songs on warm evenings. This is the best time to spot them.
seasonality.winter: Adults die with the first hard frosts, leaving behind eggs that will survive the winter embedded in woody plant material.

funFact: Unlike many insects that hear through their sides, katydids have tiny 'ears' located on their front legs just below the 'knee' joint — you can actually see these small oval hearing organs if you look closely at a live specimen with a magnifying glass!
confusionNotes: Northern bush katydids are easily confused with other bush katydids in the same genus, especially the fork-tailed and broad-winged species. The key difference is often in the tail end — look at the shape of the appendages at the tip of the abdomen, though this requires close examination and some experience to distinguish reliably.
contextualKnowledge: The genus Scudderia is named after Samuel Hubbard Scudder, a 19th-century American entomologist who was one of the first scientists to seriously study North American grasshoppers and katydids. Don't be confused by the term 'long-horned grasshopper' — katydids aren't grasshoppers at all, but the old common name stuck because of their jumping ability.
compareHints: Among the Scudderia bush katydids in New England, the northern species tends to be more common in cooler, northern areas compared to its relatives. The fork-tailed bush katydid has distinctly forked tail appendages, while the broad-winged species has noticeably wider wings. Without close examination of these subtle features, bush katydids in this genus are very difficult to distinguish and often require expert identification.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its bush katydid relatives in New England, the Fork-tailed is distinguished by that telltale forked rear appendage - Northern Bush Katydids have curved tails, while Broad-winged Bush Katydids have notably wider wings and straight tail projections.
Among New England's bush katydids, the treetop bush katydid is distinguished by its prominent dark wing stripes and preference for high canopy living.
